**Answer: 104**

**Setup.** Let $T(n)$ be the tower of $n$ twos, so $T(1)=2$, $T(2)=4$, $T(3)=16$, $T(4)=65536$, and $T(n+1)=2^{T(n)}$. Let $a_0=100$ and $a_{k+1}=a_k!$. The right-hand side is $a_{100}$, and we need the smallest $n$ with $T(n)>a_{100}$.

**Claim:** $T(k+3) < a_k < T(k+4)$ for all $k\ge 0$.

**Base case.** $T(3)=16<100<65536=T(4)$.

**Upper bound.** Suppose $a_k<T(j)$ with $j\ge 4$. Using $x!\le x^x$,
$$\log_2 a_{k+1} < T(j)\log_2 T(j) = T(j)\,T(j-1).$$
We want this to be less than $T(j+1)=2^{T(j)}$. Taking $\log_2$ of both sides, this is $T(j-1)+T(j-2)<T(j)$, which holds for $j\ge 4$ (for example, $16+4<65536$). So $a_{k+1}<T(j+1)$.

**Lower bound.** Suppose $a_k>T(j)$ with $j\ge 3$. Using $x!>(x/e)^x$,
$$\log_2 a_{k+1} > T(j)\bigl(T(j-1)-\log_2 e\bigr).$$
This exceeds $T(j)$ when $T(j-1)-\log_2 e>1$, i.e. $T(j-1)>2.44$, which holds since $T(j-1)\ge 4$. So $\log_2 a_{k+1}>T(j)$, which means $a_{k+1}>2^{T(j)}=T(j+1)$.

Both bounds propagate by induction, so the claim holds.

**Conclusion.** Taking $k=100$ gives $T(103)<a_{100}<T(104)$. Therefore $T(103)$ is not larger than the right-hand side, but $T(104)$ is. The smallest such $n$ is $104$.

ANSWER: 104
